av_event.line_text: No, I do. The household budget, every month. My wife laughs at me.
av_event.what: A young woman in a hospital pharmacy uniform with a lanyard walks across the background behind Usman, from the right edge of the frame past the bookshelf, and out of shot to the left; Usman doesn't turn round.

text:
A: Hello. Can you hear me alright?
B: Yes, hello. I can hear you fine. I'm Usman.
A: Karen. Nice to meet you. This is my third one of these, so I'm getting the hang of it now.
B: Me too. It goes quickly, three minutes.
A: It does. I've just got going and the thing cuts me off. Where are you?
B: Ilford, in East London.
A: Stourbridge. West Midlands. Black Country, if anybody asks, not Birmingham.
B: Okay. I'll remember that.
A: Good. So what do you do? You've got some very serious-looking books behind you.
B: Ah, yes, those are my old study manuals. I'm an accountant. Audit. I'm a senior manager at a firm near Liverpool Street, mostly manufacturing and logistics clients.
A: So you're the one who goes through everybody's numbers and finds the holes.
B: Er, sort of, yes. We check the accounts are right. If something doesn't add up, we ask questions.
A: I'd be a nightmare client. I'd argue every point.
B: Some clients do. It's fine, as long as they have the evidence.
A: That's fair. I'm the same with my contractors, to be honest. I manage repairs for a housing association, forty-odd operatives and contractors and a budget that's never big enough. Every month I'm sat there with my spreadsheet going, right, why has this job cost three times what it should, and who signed it off? And nine times out of ten nobody can tell me.
B: That's basically audit. You would be good at it.
A: I haven't got the qualifications. No degree. I started at the council housing office at eighteen and worked up.
B: Er, honestly, the qualifications teach you the rules. The asking questions part, some people have it and some don't. I have juniors with very good degrees who don't ask anything.
A: Well. That's a nice thing to say. I'll take that.
B: It's true.
A: Are you in the office, or at home today?
B: Home today. Three days in, two at home. The Central line in the mornings is very rammed, so the home days are good.
A: I've got the A491. Same thing really, just sat in a car instead of stood up. I get through a true crime podcast a week on it.
B: I listen to Quran recitation on the train, mostly. And some old Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, because my dad used to play it.
A: That's a lot calmer than mine. Mine's all murders. Do you do spreadsheets at home as well, or is that just me?
B: No, I do. The household budget, every month. My wife laughs at me.
A: Steve's the same with me. I do the holidays down to the minute. Printed boarding passes, the lot, in case the phone dies.
B: That's sensible, actually. Where do you go?
A: Spain or Portugal usually, one week. We did a Rhine cruise for our twenty-fifth and I loved it, which I didn't expect. What about you?
B: Mostly Lahore, to see my parents, once a year. And two years ago my wife and I did Umrah, in Mecca. That was the most important trip, for me.
A: I can imagine. I'm Church of England, I don't go every week, but I know what you mean about some things mattering more than a beach.
B: Yes. Exactly. The beach is nice, but
